claims.text: The starting material has nominal FeCoNiTi composition.
Rapid quenching produces a dual-phase fcc and hexagonal C14 Laves microstructure.
Coexistence of the C14 phase enhances coercivity to approximately 667 Oe at 400 K.
There is strong antiferromagnetic coupling between the Ti-rich C14 sublattice and the Fe/Co/Ni-rich fcc sublattice.
Interphase antiferromagnetic coupling suppresses the net saturation magnetization of the fcc phase.
The fcc/C14 phase boundaries provide a high density of magnetic domain-wall pinning sites.
Ti 3d orbitals hybridize with Fe, Co, and Ni 3d orbitals across the fcc/C14 interface.
Lattice mismatch at the fcc/C14 interface creates strong domain-wall pinning potentials.
Magnetic discontinuity at the fcc/C14 interface creates strong domain-wall pinning potentials.
The hexagonal symmetry of the C14 phase induces local magnetocrystalline anisotropy.
C14-associated magnetocrystalline anisotropy propagates into the adjacent fcc phase.
Interfacial pinning and anisotropy collectively raise coercivity above the 100 Oe limit attributed to single-phase fcc alloys.
Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni alloys have coercivity capped at 100 Oe because of insufficient orbital moments.
Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni alloys lack strong domain-wall pinning mechanisms.
The alloy exhibits magnetic ordering transitions near 1084 K, 214 K, and 168 K.
At 400 K, the alloy remains within a magnetically ordered regime relevant to the stated transitions.
The dual-phase alloy will have lower saturation magnetization than a single-phase fcc counterpart.
The proposed mechanism may not operate if the C14 phase is amorphous.
The proposed mechanism may not operate when the C14 volume fraction is below a pinning percolation threshold.
The proposed mechanism may not operate if Ti-to-Fe/Co/Ni coupling is ferromagnetic rather than antiferromagnetic.

contradictions.description: Set B is ambiguously defined as either C14-dominant or single-phase fcc, which are materially different controls, but the falsification rule subsequently treats Set B specifically as C14-dominant.
